text: Old Faithful's eruptions. Data first, the closest bell is this one. Swap the order. If closeness is a distance, order can't matter. It stays at one. Or does the closest bell move to two or to three? The D is KL divergence, named for callback and lie blur. Every maximum likelihood fit shrinks it with the data first. Much of Bayesian machine learning shrinks it with the order flipped. It's often called a distance, so treat it as one. Data first, this bell is 0.76 bits away. Shift it or stretch it, and that number only grows, so bell A is the closest. But a distance reads the same both ways. Put the bell first, and the same two curves are 1.7 bits apart, more than twice as far. Only the order changed, so the formula must care about order. To see why, take one eruption two minutes long. The data's curve stands this high there. Call it P. The bell gives it Q, about a quarter as much. Double Q twice and you reach P. So log base two of P over Q is about two, two doublings or two bits. Do that at every length. Then weight each by P, how often eruptions last that long, and add it all up. where the bell rises above the data. The gray dips pay a little back. That's the divergence, the same 0.76. Try a bell that skips the short eruptions. At two minutes it falls short by 18 and a half doublings More than a third of all eruptions are short so the bill comes to 5 bits Now keep that bill. For a second bill, swap the order. Every P trades places with Q. The bell supplies the lengths, and the data judges them. Which bell wins now? Take bell B first. It almost never imagines a short eruption, so ignoring them costs nothing. It pays 0.62. Bell A imagines eruptions in the gap and the tails, where the data has almost none. That's its 1.7. Now let Bell A slide downhill on the Bell First bill. As that bill drains, the other swells and the bell settles into B, less than half as wide. Flip the order and the closest bell moves to three. Maximum likelihood puts the data first, so a one-bell fit stretches over every hump. Variational inference approximates a Bayesian posterior with the model first, so it tends to settle on one hump. Bly and colleagues note that variational inference, generally, underestimates posterior variance. In a real ad conversion model, its average for one effect matched MCMC, but its spread was only a fifth as wide. Against raw points, with the bell first, every score is infinite, so the data must be smoothed. Smooth it more heavily and the gap partly fills. The best fit spreads almost back to A. Bell A never misses an eruption that happens. Bell B. almost never imagines one that doesn't.
